newsitem.title: UK: One year on, tears and anger among CJD sufferers.
newsitem.headline: One year on, tears and anger among CJD sufferers.

text.p: Mourning relatives of victims of the human version of mad cow disease attacked the British government on Thursday, the first anniversary of its announcement that eating infected beef might kill humans.
Tears and anger dominated a meeting of family members and carers with leading scientific experts to discuss the fatal brain-wasting disease, Creutzfeldt-Jacob Disease (CJD).
The survivors blame the government for consistently telling the public there was no risk of contracting CJD by eating beef contaminated with BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy).
"It is as though the government murdered my partner," said Marie Lawrence, who nursed her partner Mike as he died of CJD last year.
"They might just as well have picked up a gun and shot him through the head," she added, fingers trembling around a cigarette as she fought back tears.

Nearly 200 people gathered at the conference, which was organised by the CJD Support Network -- a lobby group for those caring for victims of CJD. Families shared their experiences with one another and grilled researchers in the field.

"This is really for the families so we can share with them our knowledge and try to make these dreadful events a little more bearable," explained Professor John Pattison, chairman of the Spongiform Encephalopathy Advisory Council.
Nods and anxious looks of understanding passed between audience members as Pattison outlined the symptoms of the disease that slowly eats away at the human brain.
"Many of you know these symptoms all too well," he said. Some of the listeners clutched photographs of loved ones as he spoke.
As late as November 1995, Chief Medical Officer Kenneth Calman said: "There is currently no evidence that BSE can be transmitted to humans or that eating beef causes CJD."
But on March 20, 1996, researchers announced that 10 cases of a new kind of CJD had been identified and the only cause they could think of was eating infected beef.
Health Minister Stephen Dorrell then informed parliament, triggering a storm of protest and a worldwide ban on British beef exports by the European Union.

Scientists at Thursday's conference emphasised that, while the case for a definitive link between eating beef and contracting the disease had strengthened, they still did not completely understand the disease or know how many people could have been infected by eating beef.
Estimates of potential victims range from several hundred to tens of thousands because the disease's incubation period is not known, though it is thought to range between 10 and 20 years.

"The assumption has to be that there is a causal link between CJD and BSE. The evidence has substantially strengthened in the last year," said Professor Peter Smith, adviser to the CJD Surveillance Unit. "But the bottom line is we simply don't know."

Upon hearing those words Gerard Callaghan, whose brother Maurice died from CJD, jumped to his feet and shouted: "Come off the fence and stop pissing about. It is a disgrace to say there is no final evidence."
"We have been subjected to the most concentrated official indifference and have had to bear the most crass insensitivity at times. This has to stop," Callaghan said.
At the top of the survivors' list of demands is an official inquiry into events leading up to the announcement that mad cow disease could indeed pass to humans in the form of CJD.
David Churchill, whose son Stephen was the youngest to die of CJD, called for those responsible to be brought to justice. "It's like they murdered my son, albeit by incompetence."
